text: A data breach is unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, or destruction of protected data. Organizations that handle this well follow roughly the same lifecycle — this lesson walks through it.

Detect — a monitoring alert or an unusual pattern in the audit log. Contain — stop the ongoing exposure before you fully understand it: revoke a credential, isolate a system. Assess — what data, how many people, how serious — which depends entirely on the audit trail and classification labels already being in place. Then notify, and remediate the actual cause.

A real response pulls in roles that rarely work together day to day: security for investigation and containment, legal and a privacy officer for notification obligations, communications for what gets said, and leadership for decisions that carry risk beyond any one team. The plan that was never rehearsed gets discovered incomplete in the middle of an actual incident.

GDPR's breach notification framework sets out two separate obligations. Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay, and within seventy-two hours where feasible — unless the breach is unlikely to pose a risk. Separately, if the breach is likely high-risk to individuals, you also notify those individuals directly. Not every breach triggers both.
That closes Chapter Five. Chapter Six applies everything from this course to one fictional scenario, starting with a security and privacy case study on customer data.
